evidence.note: Agent explicitly rejected incremental work and chose a monolithic push: 'Write the complete Rust application... generate the entire main.rs file at once' — the opposite of ordered shippable milestones.
The recurring 'Plan:' fields are rolling tactical to-dos (read this file, then that one), with no milestone hierarchy, no dependency/risk sequencing rationale, and no per-milestone done-checks.
A working /_health skeleton appeared, but only as a byproduct of the whole monolithic build compiling — not a deliberately sequenced skeleton-before-features milestone.
Multipart upload stubbed out to unblock the build; a defer, but there's no tracked milestone to return to it, and it was not restored.

Hard subsystems (FTS5 search, comments, path routing) were surfaced and fixed reactively during end-phase testing rather than de-risked early; endpoint checks form only a rough post-hoc verification order.

reasoning: The agent explicitly pursued a single monolithic build rather than an ordered hierarchy of shippable milestones, and its planning consisted of rolling tactical to-dos with no dependency/risk sequencing rationale or per-milestone completion criteria — matching anchor [3]'s 'vague to-do list of features.' It falls short of [5] because there was no genuine subsystem decomposition or skeleton-before-features strategy; the working skeleton and the end-phase endpoint checks emerged reactively from the monolithic build rather than from deliberate ordering, and the hardest pieces (FTS5, job queue) were never de-risked up front.
